overview.text:
Bihar takes its name from 'vihara', a Buddhist monastery, and it is the birthplace of both Buddhism and Jainism. The Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, taught on the hills of Rajgir, and Nalanda grew into one of the ancient world's great universities. Foreign tourist visits reached 0.737 million in 2024, up 35% on the year before.

Patna, the state capital, was once Pataliputra, and its Takhat Sri Harimandir Ji Patna Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh, is revered by Sikhs. Bihar's living culture is just as distinctive: Madhubani painting, made by women of the Mithila region, and Chhath, the festival to the Sun God, usually between late October and mid-November.

images.caption: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi

overview.text:
India's capital is one of its oldest cities. The Ministry of Tourism counts eight historic cities within it, each built over the ruins of the last, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Shah Jahan's Red Fort, the 12th-century Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb, the garden mausoleum that inspired the Taj Mahal.

For most international travellers Delhi is also the start of the trip: Indira Gandhi International has been India's busiest airport since 2009, and the city is the first stop on the classic Golden Triangle with Agra and Jaipur. Give it at least two days. Spend one in Old Delhi — the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid and the lanes of Chandni Chowk — and one in New Delhi and the south, from Humayun's Tomb and India Gate to the Qutub complex.

Timing matters here more than in most cities. October to March is the comfortable season, summers are very hot, and winter brings fog and, often, heavy smog. Several big sights close one day a week, so check the visiting information below before you fix your days.

best_time.text:
Winter (November–March): the cool season and the best for sightseeing; January averages about 14 °C, but fog and haze are heavy, and December fog can delay flights and trains.

Summer (April–June): very hot — averages near 38 °C in late May and early June, with heat waves up to 45 °C.

Monsoon (late June–mid-September): the rains, about 800 mm in all.

Autumn (late September–October): the post-monsoon season, cooling from about 29 to 21 °C; the cooler months begin in October.

Winter (November–February): the season starts in November, and January days in the north stay around 15–18 °C.

Summer (March–June): above 34.6 °C across the state; Gwalior, Morena and Datia pass 42 °C in May.

Monsoon (mid-June–September): the southwest monsoon breaks in mid-June and brings most of the year's rain.

items.body: Sarafa Bazaar, Indore — India's only night street-food market.
Chappan Dukan, Indore — one of the city's best-known street-food spots.
Indore namkeen — the city's famous savoury snacks.
Indore cooking — a mix of Maharashtrian, Malwi, Rajasthani and Gujarati flavours.
Khajuraho Dance Festival — classical dance beside the temples, 20–26 February.
Tansen Samaroh — Hindustani music near Gwalior, every December.
Shoes off — leave them at the door of temples and mosques; socks are fine.
Right hand — eat, pass and accept things with your right hand.
Dress — cover your legs and shoulders, especially at places of worship.
Photos — don't photograph deities or temple interiors unless it's clearly allowed.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Indore is the busiest airport, followed by Bhopal; Gwalior also has flights.

By rail: a 4,948 km network with 20 major junctions — about 220 trains a day pass through Bhopal alone.

By road: buses reach most of the state.

overview.text: Odisha has over 480 km of coastline and more than 62 tribal groups. Puri's Jagannath Temple is one of the Char Dhams; the Konark Sun Temple is a UNESCO site; Bhubaneswar is a city of temples; and Chilika is Asia's largest coastal lagoon.

Summer (March–May): the hot pre-monsoon months.

places.name: Uttar Pradesh
places.summary: India's most visited state for domestic travellers, home to the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Varanasi and the newly inscribed Sarnath.
places.seoTitle: Uttar Pradesh Travel Guide: Agra, Varanasi & Sarnath
places.seoDescription: Plan a trip to Uttar Pradesh: the Taj Mahal and Agra's Mughal monuments, Varanasi's ghats and the UNESCO-listed Buddhist site of Sarnath.

images.alt: Boats on the Ganga in front of Dashashwamedh Ghat in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh
images.caption: Dashashwamedh Ghat, Varanasi

overview.text:
Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state in India and, by the Ministry of Tourism's count, the most visited: it recorded 646.81 million domestic tourist visits in 2024, more than a fifth of the national total, along with 2.27 million foreign tourist visits. Lucknow is the state capital, but most travellers come for two places in particular.

Agra holds three World Heritage Sites — the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri — and the Taj Mahal is the country's most visited ticketed monument for both Indian and foreign visitors. Further east, Varanasi sits on the Ganga, and just outside it the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2026.

Use this page as a starting point: the destination guides below cover each city in detail, with visiting rules, getting there, where to stay and ready-made itineraries.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: fly into the airport nearest your first city: Lucknow's is 14 km from the centre, Varanasi's 22 km and Ayodhya's about 10 km from Ayodhya Dham.

By rail: the state's cities are well connected by train — Shatabdi expresses run from New Delhi to Lucknow and Kanpur, and Agra Cantt, Varanasi, Prayagraj, Lucknow and Mathura are among India's 50 world-class stations.

By road: India's largest road network, with 42 national highways; the Agra and Purvanchal expressways link Lucknow with Agra and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
